feature.snow_deformation.condition_view_: Paints the ground snow with the condition at each point: higher ground is colder. Track age paints trenches and their berms from green, just cut, to red, fully aged; untouched snow stays white. Ice paints the glaze on packed snow cyan. Roads and objects keep their look.
feature.snow_deformation.corpse_marks_to: A body that is still alight, crackling or frozen over goes on working the snow it fell in - melting, pocking or glazing to match. Which one comes from whatever last struck the actor before it died, so nothing has to be read off the corpse itself. Mods that keep bodies burning or frozen long after death get the most out of this.
feature.snow_deformation.corpse_seconds_: How long a body goes on marking after it falls. Vanilla death effects fade in a couple of seconds; mods that leave a corpse visibly burning or frozen run far longer, so match this to what you can actually see rather than to anything physical.
feature.snow_deformation.creature_sink_t: Creatures lighter than you sink only part way into the snow. Where the snow is firm enough to carry them, a hare or a fox stands up to half way up it and leaves a shallower trench; in loose new snow they sink further, but never past their belly, and never into something low overhead. Your own weight is the measure: people sink as you do, and anything as heavy as you or heavier stands on the ground under the snow. A creature that dies settles into the snow. Weight comes from each creature's own collision shapes, so modded creatures work too. The same weight sets how hard a creature hits the snow: a horse's gallop or landing throws more broken snow than a fox's. Off, every creature stands on the ground and hits the snow as you do.
feature.snow_deformation.crust_break_car: How completely cutting through a crust destroys it. Anything that cuts snow has broken the skin over it, so a trench should expose loose snow rather than staying polished all the way down - at 0 the glaze survives inside tracks and they read as grooves ploughed through ice cream.
feature.snow_deformation.crust_break_rad: Only creatures that carve by stamps read this: those beyond about 44 m from you or past the 16 nearest, such as a distant mammoth or a landing dragon. It is the size a body part must reach before it breaks through a crust instead of printing on it, standing in for weight: low values let anything shatter the glaze, high values let a mammoth walk on it. Nearer creatures carve by their own mesh and always print on a crust at Frost Print Depth.
feature.snow_deformation.crust_print_dep: How deep tracks still cut into fully crusted snow, against loose snow. Deliberately not zero: actors walk on the ground while the snow layer sits above them, so a crust nothing can mark buries feet inside what looks like solid ice.
feature.snow_deformation.crust_radius_to: Reach of a frost source that states none of its own: a frost cloak, a frost atronach's aura (scaled by Frost Atronach Reach) and a body frozen where it fell (scaled by its size). A spell that authors its own area, like Blizzard, uses that instead and ignores this; a held stream keeps its own small reach.
feature.snow_deformation.crust_rate_tool: How fast frost sets a crust, for a spell of Frostbite's strength. Like a melt this changes how quickly the glaze arrives, never how hard it ends up.
feature.snow_deformation.crust_thaw_tool: How long a crust takes to melt away on its own. Ice answers to temperature rather than to weather, so this runs even under a clear sky, where snowfall has stopped and nothing else would ever remove it. 0 leaves a glaze standing until snow buries it.
feature.snow_deformation.dash_gouge_tool: Width of the furrow a shout ploughs when it throws its own caster forward, against the size of whatever is being thrown - so a dragon cuts a wider one than a man. Nothing is named here either: a self-delivered shout is simply watched for a moment, and what marks the snow is the caster moving faster than anything on foot can. A shout that leaves them standing marks nothing.
feature.snow_deformation.debug_cat_melt_: A stand-in heat source that answers to no spell at all. Kept for testing a mark on its own: when a school stops marking, this says whether the fault is in the detector or in the mark itself.
feature.snow_deformation.debug_hint: Deformation map: red = compressed snow. The window is centred on the camera, so the cross is you and the ring is 25 m.
feature.snow_deformation.debug_inject_hi: Trench store: what the inject last painted into the window. Opaque, so what you see is what the store holds. Refreshed when the window scrolls or is rebuilt - after a load it is the whole restored window.
feature.snow_deformation.debug_log_all_j: Writes every object's capture verdict to CommunityShaders.log as 'ice journey' lines - mesh name, flags, texture path and which gate accepted or rejected it - once per object and outcome while ticked. Swaying trees and distant LOD are left out. Tick, look at the object in question, untick; then search the log for its mesh name. An object with no line at all never reached the capture.
feature.snow_deformation.debug_overlay_t: Paints diagnostics on terrain: red = outside deformation window, green = deformation, blue = detected snow.
feature.snow_deformation.debug_proj_albe: Paints classified projected snow with the snow texture the recolor JUST SAMPLED, raw and unshaded, in place of blending it in. The magenta view cannot answer this: it replaces the sample with a constant, so it proves the block runs and its weight, and nothing about the texture. Snow here means the sample is good and the recolor is failing further on; the object's own rock or black means the shell snow texture is not reaching the draw.
feature.snow_deformation.debug_proj_snow: Tints every pixel the projected-snow match classifies and replaces in magenta. If a snowy rock or fence shows no magenta, the classification missed that draw; if the magenta area is wrong, the projection weight is. The counters below break last frame's draws down; every projected material record seen is also logged to CommunityShaders.log.
feature.snow_deformation.debug_proj_weig: Paints the game's projected snow with the weight the recolor really blends by, black = none to white = solid; projected surfaces the recolor does not treat as snow turn red. Turn object snow off and compare with the Object Snow Debug View's Projected mask mode (its red channel is the skin's own reconstruction of the same weight): wherever the two disagree is where the shell or its coat paints what the game does not.
feature.snow_deformation.decals_on_objec: Scorch, frost and shock marks and rune glyphs are decals the game lays on a surface, and the thin snow coat on rocks and walls is drawn on top of them. With this on they are put back over the coat, as blood is. Bare rock is left alone.
feature.snow_deformation.description: Maintains a persistent deformation map around the player so snow can be visibly compressed by actors moving through it, leaving lasting trails.
feature.snow_deformation.distant_snow_to: Snow on far terrain the game hasn't loaded: heights come from the worldspace heightmap (shipped with Community Shaders), and snow placement follows the game's own distant LOD textures — where the LOD is painted snowy, our snow appears. Loaded terrain always uses its real snow textures instead. The sliders here also set how far each snow system reaches; higher = more VRAM and GPU cost.
feature.snow_deformation.edge_lump_reach: How far the snow on rocks and buildings reaches past the patches the game paints, onto the bare surface. At 0 it is exactly the game's paint. Raising it lets the snow creep outward along the game's own falloff - slope, painted alpha and the projection's noise - so thin dustings thicken first and steep faces stay bare longest. The same from every angle. Needs Recolor Projected Snow, and only objects that carry the game's own projected-snow data take part.
feature.snow_deformation.effect_cost_pro: Turns each snow shading effect off in turn for about two seconds and shows how much GPU time the snow saves without it. Covers the ground snow and the snow on objects, which share these effects. Stand still and keep the camera still while it runs (about 50 seconds); the effects visibly switch off one by one. Differences under about 0.03 ms are measurement noise.
feature.snow_deformation.enable_accumula: Let snowfall deepen the snow. Off holds every kind of ground at its set depth whatever the weather does, which is how the mod behaved before this existed - useful for comparing the two.
feature.snow_deformation.flatten_paralla: The other answer to snow floating over parallax objects: on an object with projected snow, its Extended Materials parallax (PBR displacement and complex parallax) fades out as the snow covers the surface, the way real snow fills cracks and crevices, and the shadows the relief casts on itself fade with it. Where the snow lies solid the rock is flat, so the snow, its coat and the tracks in it sit on a surface that does not move; where it lies in patches part of the relief stays; bare rock keeps all of it. With Snow Follows Parallax also on, the patches follow the relief that stays. Objects on the older vanilla parallax shader carry no projected snow and are not affected. On by default, together with the other one.
feature.snow_deformation.floating_band_t: Far field only (the bone path beyond the contact window, about 44 m). How far an actor's lowest part may sit above its footing and still count as standing on it. Lower values catch things that only just hover, at the risk of dropping a normal creature's tracks mid-stride.
feature.snow_deformation.force_carve_dep: How deep a full-strength shove ploughs at the mouth, as a fraction of the layer; the mark gets shallower from there. Each shout scales down from here by the impact force its own record carries, so a dragon's shout bites harder than a breath's shove without either being named.
feature.snow_deformation.force_track_dep: How deep a travelling shove scours, against a full carve. A vortex scours the surface rather than digging to the ground - and the raised rim is derived from how deep the cut goes, so this is the dial that decides whether the trail reads as a scoured hollow or as a canyon with a ridge down each side.
feature.snow_deformation.force_track_too: Width of the trail left by a shove slow enough to watch travel - a cyclone rather than a shockwave. Those are told apart by speed alone: every shout blast crosses its own reach in about a second, while a cyclone crawls at barely above a sprint and takes four, so it leaves the line it took instead of a wedge. Nothing authors a width for it any more than for a cone, so this is taste.
feature.snow_deformation.fresh_snow_sett: How long clear weather takes to turn loose new snow fully firm. About two game hours of heavy snowfall makes it fully fresh again; lighter snow takes longer.
feature.snow_deformation.fresh_snow_soft: New snow is loose: it cannot hold a cut wall, and it packs down under a boot instead of being thrown aside. While it snows, and for a while after, the ridge beside trenches shrinks and the rim loses its lip and teeth; trenches cut by distant creatures, spells and shouts also get sloped sides instead of sharp walls. As the snow settles over the following days, the look you set with Berm Height, Rim Lip and Rim Teeth comes back and those walls sharpen again; a trench keeps the walls it was cut with. 0 = off, the snow is always firm. Snow Climate takes over from this as it rises: at 1.00 fresh snow acts through its stickiness and density instead.
feature.snow_deformation.freshness_overr: Not saved. Below 0 the weather drives the snow's freshness; at 0 or above this value replaces it, so firm (0) and fresh (1) can be compared on the spot without waiting for a storm. The ridge and rim change at once; wall steepness only shows on trenches cut after the change.
feature.snow_deformation.frost_decals_to: A frost spell leaves the game's own frost mark where it lands, and the landscape snow covers the ones on the ground beneath it. With this on, the mark is painted onto the snow over it, lit as the game lights the decal, and fades with it: on the landscape and road snow, and with Spell Marks Over Object Snow on object snow lying on what the mark covers, such as a walkway the snow pokes through.
feature.snow_deformation.horizon_snow_to: Recolors the game's distant LOD terrain with the shell's own snow material wherever its bake reads as snow, so snow appearance stays consistent from your feet to the horizon. The snow shell ends at the loaded-cell boundary and this takes over from there, out to the edge of the world.
feature.snow_deformation.impact_reach_to: How far the impact detail spreads around a hard hit - a sprint, a dodge, a landing, a body knocked down - as a share of what hit the snow. At 1 a foot's impact covers its own print and a thin ring around it, and a body knocked down an area about its own size; 2 is twice as wide. The snow it throws is Speed Spoil's. Applies to new impacts.
feature.snow_deformation.incorporeal_mod: Stops things with no substance from digging the snow. This is a separate question from hovering, and has to be: a ghost stands with its feet on the ground like the Nord it otherwise is, so no clearance measurement will ever catch one. See-through bodies judges an actor by whether it is drawn solid, which needs no list and covers modded ghosts; actors marked Ghost reads the flag on the record instead, which never misses a ghost but also catches anything the game made unkillable rather than incorporeal.
feature.snow_deformation.item_embed_tool: How far a heavy dropped item presses into the floor of the trench it lands in, as a share of its own thickness. Shape decides how much of this an item takes: rounded items (armor, buckets, boots) take all of it, flat ones (shields, swords, books) almost none, so they stay in view. Light items rest on the snow whatever this is. 0 = every item rests on its trench floor.
feature.snow_deformation.item_min_roundn: How rounded an item must be before it presses into its trench floor at all. Roundness is an item's thickness against the width of its largest side: a greatsword is about 0.08, a book 0.15, a shield 0.24, boots 0.6, a bucket 0.9. Items at or under this value rest on the floor; the share grows from here to the full Dropped Item Sink at 0.5. Raise it if flat items still disappear, lower it to let them sink.
feature.snow_deformation.item_sink_toolt: A dropped item rests in the snow at a depth set by its weight and size: a ring stays on the surface, a shield goes to the bottom of the trench it cuts. Off, every item falls to the ground under the snow, as the game places it. Items stay where physics left them either way, so picking them up is unchanged.
feature.snow_deformation.item_snow_grip_: Snow packs under what drops into it and stops it rolling. The deeper an item is in the snow and the slower it is travelling, the harder it is held: dropped straight into deep snow it stays where it lands, thrown hard it still slides until it slows, and in shallow snow it rolls almost as it would on bare ground. 0 = the game's own physics.
feature.snow_deformation.key_feature_1: Persistent world-space deformation map following the player
feature.snow_deformation.key_feature_2: Trails carved by the player, NPCs and creatures
feature.snow_deformation.land_recolor_to: Where the land itself shows (prints down to the ground, thin snow, the bases of blended objects), its snow textures wear this mod's snow, texel by texel. Rocks, grass and dirt inside those textures keep their own look.
feature.snow_deformation.lift_frost_tool: Lifts a wall of frost, and the small ice effects like it, up onto the snow standing over them instead of leaving them buried underneath it. Frost is the only school this happens to: fire melts its own hole and lightning pits one, so those sit in snow they have already taken away, while frost only hardens what is there and leaves the full layer on top of itself. This is the one thing in the whole feature that MOVES something belonging to the game, so it has its own switch.
feature.snow_deformation.lift_runes_tool: Lifts a rune's shimmer, glow and cast flash onto the snow standing over them, so they play at the painted glyph rather than under it. Ground runes only - one cast on a wall stays where it is. What sets a rune off does not move: it still triggers from the ground.
feature.snow_deformation.lightning_arcs_: Draws the bolt between a lightning cloak's wearer and the ground it just struck. Without it the snow pocks with nothing reaching the spot, which reads as a glitch rather than as lightning. Purely visual - nothing is spawned into the world, no damage, no sound.
feature.snow_deformation.lod_object_snow: Distant objects the game draws as LOD without its projected-snow flags - snow drifts, snowy roads, piles - keep their own baked snow texture, which reads far brighter than the shell. This applies the Horizon Snow recolor to those pixels too, with the same detection slider below.
feature.snow_deformation.lod_snow_sensit: How eagerly a distant LOD texture pixel counts as snow. The scale was widened: the old best-at-1.0 now sits near 0.5. Low = only bright white; high = pale gray rock starts counting too. The same setting drives the Horizon Snow recolor, so it decides where snow sits on the far terrain as well as how the shell reads it.
feature.snow_deformation.map_resolution_: Resolution of the map every trench, melt mark and berm lives in. The main performance dial for this section: cost scales with the square of it, so each step down roughly quarters the trench passes' GPU time. Detail follows the Trenches range too - at the default range, 2048 gives roughly 12 cm per texel, 1024 roughly 24 cm (footprints soften but trails stay). 4096 halves the texel again and costs roughly four times 2048's trench-pass time and video memory; the High preset uses it. Changing it clears the map; remembered trenches are re-injected from the store.
feature.snow_deformation.melt_bowl_floor: Shape of a melted hollow. 0 curves from the centre like a bowl, which is how heat actually spreads; higher values hold a flat floor and stand the sides up into walls, which reads as blasted rather than melted. Every frost glaze takes the same profile: higher holds the full glaze further out before it fades.
feature.snow_deformation.melt_edge_irreg: How far a melted rim wanders off a perfect circle. This moves the outline only and leaves the surface smooth - a melt basin has a wandering edge but no jagged shards. The edge of every frost glaze wanders by the same amount.
feature.snow_deformation.melt_emitter_ra: Depth melted per second at the bowl core. At 1.0 the core reaches full depth in a second; low values make the deepening easy to watch.
feature.snow_deformation.melt_persistenc: How much longer melted ground stays bare than trampled ground. The ground under a fire is warm and wet after the flame is gone, so a melt basin outlasts a footprint of the same depth. 0 = both recover at the same rate.
feature.snow_deformation.model_depths_to: Object snow: the recolor of the game's projected snow and the dials that shape the drape over it. Flat vs round is classified automatically per mesh.
feature.snow_deformation.multipass_snow_: Objects whose snow material is drawn in two passes (vanilla glaciers and ice sheets, and every snow object under Simplicity of Snow) keep the drape only where the game's own snow pass paints. Off, the drape guesses on them and covers every face, stone included.
feature.snow_deformation.name: Snow Deformation
feature.snow_deformation.no_carve_floati: Far field only. Inside the contact window (about 44 m) an actor carves by its render mesh, and anything that hovers reaches no snow by construction; this gate covers the bone path beyond it. Stops things that never touch the ground from digging it: atronachs, wisps, ghosts, anything that hovers. Nothing is named - an actor is judged by whether its own lowest part ever comes down to its footing, so modded levitators are covered too.
feature.snow_deformation.object_meet_ban: Where the ground snow meets a snow-covered object, the two blend toward each other so they read as one surface instead of meeting at a lit line. This is the width of that meeting, split in half: at the default 12, the ground snow's shading eases toward the object's slope over its last 6 units, and the object's snow eases toward the ground's over the first 6 units up from it, meeting in the middle. Higher = a wider, softer meeting; 0 = off, the two meet as they are. Shading only - no geometry moves. 70 units is about a metre.
feature.snow_deformation.object_print_ri: How far past a footprint's edge the snow on objects - roofs, floorboards, rocks, logs - is broken up, in units. The trench detail (Detail Coverage, at twice Detail Relief) runs this far around each print and fades out, strongest at the print's edge. 0 = only the print's own edge.
feature.snow_deformation.object_raster_r: How far around you the top-down height map of the objects reaches. Inside it, snow thins under roofs, bridges and archways, road snow takes its shape and its trenches, footprints can be laid on objects, and Volume Snow finds what shelters it. Past it there is no shelter under cover and no footprints on objects, and road snow goes on from a coarser road-only map to the edge of the loaded cells. Keep it at or above the reach of Snow Trenches on Objects, or footprints on objects stop at this range. The map is a fixed 2048 texels however far it reaches, so this trades detail against range: a texel is about 7 world units at the default 100 m, 4 at 58 m. Costs nothing extra to raise; it coarsens the map near you instead.
feature.snow_deformation.object_snow_nea: Near you - over a quarter of the Object Height Map Range, 25 m at its default - road snow and the trenches in it read their shape from a map four times finer: about 1.7 world units a texel instead of 6.8 at the default range. Off, roads use the coarser map everywhere: slightly softer road edges and trenches up close, a little less GPU time. The Medium and Low presets turn it off.
feature.snow_deformation.object_trench_r: How far around you footprints in the snow on objects - roofs, floorboards, rocks, logs, bridges - are kept: 11, 22 or 44 m. They are always on. Like trenches in the ground they refill while it snows, and with Remember Trenches on they are kept when you walk away and saved with the game. The print map takes 2, 8 or 32 MB of video memory. Changing it keeps remembered footprints and drops the last moments not yet stored.
feature.snow_deformation.parallax_depth_: Parallax occlusion mapping on the landscape shell: marches the view ray through the snow texture's displacement map and shades from where it hits, so grain occludes grain and the surface reads as thick instead of merely lit. It moves no vertices, and the depth it resolves is by construction the depth of the grain being drawn. A multiplier on the PBR config's displacementScale - 1.0 is exactly the slab depth PBR ground gets. 0 skips the march. It also sets how strongly the trench detail shades itself from the sun: 0 turns that off, 1 or more gives it in full.
feature.snow_deformation.parallax_shadow: Self-shadowing of the snow's own grain, the same term PBR ground receives from Extended Materials: four taps along the sun through the displacement map, so the micro-relief casts into itself under low sun instead of reading flat. Needs the PBR snow set's _p map. 0 skips the taps entirely (and is the A/B for their cost). It scales the trench detail's own sun shadow the same way: 0 turns that off too.
feature.snow_deformation.persist_accumul: How deep the layer has grown is written to the save and comes back with it, so loading in the middle of a week-long winter finds the world as deep as you left it. Off, every load starts at the authored depth and the layer has to build again from whatever the sky is doing - which is also what to use when comparing, since the depth then depends only on the weather since the load.
feature.snow_deformation.persist_trenche: Trenches survive leaving the area. Snow deformation is drawn in a window that follows the camera, and without this everything outside it is discarded: walk a few hundred metres away and your trail is gone when you come back. On, departing ground is kept in a sparse store, put back on return, and written to the save so it is still there after a reload. Off restores the old behaviour and frees the store.
feature.snow_deformation.pit_depth_toolt: How deep a discharge pocks the snow, as a fraction of the layer: at 1 a full strike throws its deepest pocks clear to the ground, and the pocking leaves shallower snow between them. Unlike a melt it does not deepen with time, however long a cloak crackles over one spot.
feature.snow_deformation.pit_radius_tool: Reach of a single discharge before its arc legs, which fork out past it. Bigger spells scale up from here.
feature.snow_deformation.proj_snow_match: Makes the game's painted-on projected snow look like this mod's snow, and owns the DRAPE that does it. Two halves: inside the object's own shader the projection's texture and material are swapped for the snow shell's set, which works from every angle, overhangs included; and near the camera the shell lays its own material over the parts the game paints solidly, which is what gives the drape the shell's snow rather than a tint of it. Edge Lump Reach shapes that second half - how far it spreads past the paint. Every pixel the game paints solidly (its own half blend and up) takes the full snow, all or nothing; a faint dusting stays bare. The drape lies flat on the mesh; nothing of ours stands above an object. Only draws whose projected material really is snow are touched, so sand and moss projections keep their look.
feature.snow_deformation.proj_snow_norma: Recolored projected snow also takes the snow's own surface relief, perturbed exactly the way the drape's coat does, so the drape and the bare snow beside it share one grain. Without it the game's projected snow keeps the plank's or the stone's own bump - the game never sends its own snow normal to the deferred buffer - and the snow reads as paint on the surface wherever the drape does not cover it.
feature.snow_deformation.quality_presets: Sets the performance settings in one click. High is the default: every effect on, every reach at its maximum and a 4096 Deformation Map. Medium keeps the snow's shadows (Snow Casts Shadows, Snow Self-Shadowing) and turns off the close-up extras (Snow Sparkle, Snow Contact Shadows, Object Snow Near Detail), with Trenches at 115 m, NPC Trenches at 105 m, Object Snow at 150 m, a 24 px Object Snow Tessellation Cap and Snow Trenches on Objects at 22 m. Low turns all five off, and parallax too, with a 1024 Deformation Map, Trenches at 29 m, Object Snow at 50 m, NPC Trenches at 10 m, a 32 px cap and Snow Trenches on Objects at 11 m. Every preset turns Tessellate Trenches on and the experimental Volume Snow off. Everything else keeps its value; change any of these afterwards and the preset shows as Custom. Applying can clear existing trenches (a resolution or Trenches-range change does); remembered trenches are re-injected.
feature.snow_deformation.range_actor_tre: How far from the camera NPCs, creatures and corpses still carve trenches. Past it they leave no prints, and the work of following their bodies is skipped. You always carve. It never reaches past the Trenches range. Lower saves CPU time where many people or animals are on the move. Applies live.
feature.snow_deformation.range_skins_too: Capture radius for snow skins on objects (rocks, cliffs, roofs); skins dissolve softly over the last ~29 m of it. Applies live.
feature.snow_deformation.range_trenches_: Deformation window radius: you carve anywhere inside it, NPCs out to NPC Trenches. Applying a change CLEARS existing trenches. NOT a GPU setting: GPU cost follows Deformation Map Resolution, not range. Texel detail is range divided by resolution, so a smaller range at the same resolution means sharper footprints over a shorter reach.
feature.snow_deformation.recolored_snow_: The snow on rocks and buildings creeps out from its painted patches as it snows and draws back as it melts: Edge Lump Reach runs from 0 to 1 over Accumulation Time, back over Melt Time and Accumulated Snow Fade, whatever the Accumulation Peak. Off, the Edge Lump Reach slider is used as set.
feature.snow_deformation.refill_only_sno: Compressed snow only recovers while the current weather is snowing, faster in denser snowfall. Trails and trenches persist through clear weather. Off: snow recovers at the baseline rate in any weather.
feature.snow_deformation.refill_rate_too: Multiplier on the snowfall-driven refill rate. At 1.0x, typical snowfall recovers compressed snow in about 12 minutes. 0 disables refilling.
feature.snow_deformation.rim_lip_tooltip: The trench rim rolls UP slightly before it drops - the cornice look of cut snow. Height as a fraction of local snow depth; deep snow only (shallow dimples stay smooth). 0 = off.
feature.snow_deformation.rim_teeth_toolt: Breaks the trench edge into irregular teeth and blocks instead of a clean curve, from a ragged noise fixed to the ground. Deep snow only. Too high eats the trench's readable width - back off if trails start looking chewed. 0 = off.
feature.snow_deformation.road_meshes_dep: Snow layer on road meshes; bridges are ordinary objects. Kept below the surrounding snow classes so the road's course stays readable through the snowfield.
feature.snow_deformation.rune_decals_too: A rune's glyph is a decal the game lays on the ground, so deep snow covers it. With this on, the glyph is painted onto the snow over it instead, lit and glowing as the game lights the decal, and leaves with the rune: on the landscape and road snow, and with Spell Marks Over Object Snow on object snow lying on what the glyph covers.
feature.snow_deformation.scorch_strength: How dark a discharge burns the snow it struck. 0 leaves the pocking alone and removes the blackening entirely.
feature.snow_deformation.seasons_snow_ma: Steepest slope that keeps snow on objects Seasons of Skyrim paints at runtime. Those projections come with the record default of 90 degrees and no painted mask; 90 keeps Seasons' own coverage, which the recolor and the drape then follow exactly, and lower cuts the snow off steeper faces for them only. Authored snow objects keep their own angle and mask.
feature.snow_deformation.shell_horizon_m: The snow shades itself: bumps, drifts, berms and trench rims cast soft shadows onto the snow behind them, found by a short march toward the sun over the snow's height, on the ground snow and on object snow. It fades out as the sun nears the horizon, where the game's own shadows take over. Off, the snow is shaded by the game's shadows and Snow Contact Shadows only. The Low preset turns it off.
feature.snow_deformation.shell_join_need: Depth prepass join: needs Terrain Blending
feature.snow_deformation.shell_join_not_: Depth prepass join: not this frame (no ground snow or a new render size)
feature.snow_deformation.shell_join_unav: Depth prepass join: unavailable (a shader failed, or no landscape capture this frame)
feature.snow_deformation.shell_join_view: Frames whose view changed under the early pass:
feature.snow_deformation.shell_pipeline_: Hardware pipeline-statistics and occlusion queries around the ground snow's draws (when its prepass runs late, in DrawShell) and the object-snow pass, read back two frames later without stalling. PS invocations divided by samples passed is how many pixel-shader runs each visible pixel costs - overdraw times quad overshade. The DS/HS/VS counts check the geometry-stage arithmetic. A line counts all of that pass's draws - the prepass's own cheap invocations and the fullscreen passes' samples are in there - so read the profiler rows as the verdict and these lines as the explanation.
feature.snow_deformation.shell_sss_not_d: Shadow depth sync: not this frame (needs the depth prepass join drawing, Snow Contact Shadows, and Screen-Space Shadows in an exterior)
feature.snow_deformation.shelter_drift_a: Cover higher than Shelter Max Height (up to about 250 units) still keeps the snow off where the spot is enclosed - cover all around it, like the inside of a tent; a spot open along one side, like the strip under an overhang, keeps its snow. This angle is how far from straight down the snow blows in, which sets how much cover a spot needs around it to count as enclosed. Higher = snow reaches further in, so only deep cover shelters; lower = a smaller roof is enough. Default 30.
feature.snow_deformation.shelter_max_hei: Snow under a roof, bridge or archway thins out, because the structure keeps the snowfall off. A structure whose underside is higher above the ground than this no longer counts: a wide archway with plenty of air under it is as open as the sky, and the snow beneath it keeps its full depth. Fades out over the next 100 units. 70 units is about a metre.
feature.snow_deformation.shock_cloak_int: Seconds between a lightning cloak's discharges. Higher is sparser - lightning cracks now and then rather than pouring out continuously.
feature.snow_deformation.shock_cloak_rad: How far a lightning cloak throws its arcs. Kept separate from the fire cloak's reach because the two behave differently: heat wraps the body, arcs jump clear of it.
feature.snow_deformation.shock_cloak_str: Size of one arc against the cloak's own reach. Small values scatter fine pocks; large ones land marks nearly as wide as the cloak itself.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_churn_too: How broken up a shout's mark is. 0 is a smooth scoop with a clean edge. At 1 a shove throws the snow near the mouth in uneven streaks, and further out only the strongest streaks land, so the mark thins into dashes before it ends. A breath's melt or frost stays solid; only its outline turns ragged. A shout that lays this mark leaves no other - the projectile it throws does not dig.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_cones_too: Lets a shout work the whole oval of ground in front of the shouter rather than only the spot its projectile happens to strike. Each shout takes its reach from its own record, so a dragon's breath carries ten times a Greybeard's without anything being named. Off, shouts mark only through whatever they throw, and Whirlwind Sprint ploughs no furrow.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_fade_star: How far along the mark the snow is thrown to full depth before it starts getting shallower. 0 fades from the mouth; 1 holds full depth to the end.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_far_depth: Depth the mark fades to at its far end, against the depth at the mouth. What lands out there is the odd streak; this is how deep it goes.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_reach_too: Multiplier on the reach each shout's own projectile authors - about 1000 units for Unrelenting Force, 1200 for the breaths, ten times that for a dragon. The far part of the mark fades and breaks up on its own, so this sets where the last streaks end, not where the solid scoop does. Aiming upward shortens it; aiming at the sky throws it away, since the snow layer cannot hold a mark in the air.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_roundness: The outline's curve. 1 is straight-sided - a kite from the mouth to the widest point and on to the end; 2 is an oval; higher squares the sides off.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_streak_le: How much longer than wide each streak is, along the direction of the shout. 1 is blotches; higher draws them out into the lines snow thrown forward leaves.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_streak_si: Width of the streaks the churn breaks a shove's mark into, in world units. Below a couple of map texels they blur together.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_waist_too: Where along the reach the mark is widest. Low values swell it just ahead of the mouth and taper the rest; high values open it slowly and round off the far end.
feature.snow_deformation.shout_width_too: How wide the mark is at its widest, as a fraction of its reach. The records author a shout's REACH but never its width, so this is the one thing about its shape that has to be taste rather than a reading.
feature.snow_deformation.skin_cull_log_t: Writes one frame's culling verdicts to CommunityShaders.log: every skin the cull skipped, and every skin drawn in the game's decal depth mode, with its mesh name, reason and index count. Use it when the Skin identity view shows an object with no skin at all.
feature.snow_deformation.skin_depth_bias: How far the object snow layer is nudged toward the camera in the depth buffer, in the buffer's own smallest steps. The layer is rasterised from the same vertices as the object under it, so at a distance the two land on the same depth value and fight - snow that flickers, or shows from one angle and not another. A few steps settle the fight; more than needed makes the layer stand in front of things that should hide it. Constant with distance in depth terms, which is what the contest needs.
feature.snow_deformation.skin_slope_dept: The part of the depth bias that grows with how steeply a face is seen. Faces at a grazing angle cover a large depth range per pixel and fight hardest; this scales the nudge with that slope. Capped internally so no angle can push the layer far in front of its object.
feature.snow_deformation.skin_sss_not_dr: Object snow shadow march: not this frame (needs object snow on screen with its depth prepass, Snow Contact Shadows, and Screen-Space Shadows in an exterior)
feature.snow_deformation.skin_tess_cap_p: Caps how finely road snow is subdivided (no other object snow is): no subdivision segment may be smaller on screen than this many pixels. At a distance, finer segments end up smaller than a pixel and cost GPU time for nothing visible. Higher = cheaper: up to about 20 it only trims the rounded edges at range; above that it coarsens the whole road surface. 0 turns the cap off. The Medium and Low presets raise it.
feature.snow_deformation.slope_drape_too: How the ground snow stands off steep ground. At 0 it is always lifted straight up, so on a near-vertical face the cover thins to almost nothing and the rock shows through in diagonal gaps. At 1 the lift turns toward the surface as the ground steepens (from 30 degrees, fully by 60), so the layer keeps its full depth in front of the face - the way snow plasters a mountainside rather than only sitting on top of it. Snow on objects is not affected.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_accumulati: The snow layer deepens while it snows and settles back when it stops, so a long storm leaves the world deeper than it found it. Landscape snow only - snow sitting on objects keeps its fixed depth.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_casts_shad: The ground snow and road snow are drawn into the sun's shadows, so deep snow, banks and trench walls cast shadows onto the world and onto the snow itself. Off, the snow still receives shadows but casts none. The Low preset turns it off.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_climate_to: How much the kind of snow decides what a trench looks like. The snow's temperature comes from how snowy the land is, the weather, the sun and the height. At 1.00, cold powder leaves holes with no ridge and loose snow fallen back into them; settled snow just below freezing keeps the full ridge, lip and teeth; wet snow leaves dark prints with crisp walls. Berm Height, Rim Lip and Rim Teeth are the most the snow can give. At 0 the look is the fixed one set by the sliders and Fresh Snow Softness. Debugging Options > Snow Condition shows what the snow asks for.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_follows_pa: On objects drawn with Extended Materials parallax (PBR displacement and complex parallax), the snow lies on the surface the parallax draws instead of on the flat mesh under it: its edge and its own texture move with the stone as the camera moves, so the stone no longer slides beneath the snow and the snow stops looking like it floats. Both the game's recolored projected snow and the drape's coat over it follow. With Flatten Parallax Under Snow also on, they follow the relief the flatten leaves. The first time it is switched on, the coat compiles its shaders, a stall of a few seconds once. Objects on the older vanilla parallax shader are not affected. On by default, together with the other one.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_glints_too: The glitter of light catching single snow crystals, on the ground snow and on object snow, using Community Shaders' TruePBR glints (needs TruePBR). The Medium and Low presets turn it off.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_pbr_config: The shell takes its roughness, specular level and sparkle from a TruePBR texture set, matched by the snow texture's file name. A modlist often holds several sets whose name contains that word - a blend variant, a glacier, a grass edge - and some of them carry no sparkle settings at all, which leaves the snow flat and dull. Leave this empty to take the best automatic match, or type a set's name (its JSON file name, without the extension) to pin it. The set in use is shown beside this box and updates as you type.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_refill_too: How compressed snow recovers, and how deep the layer grows while it snows.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_resistance: How much of a body's push the snow holds back. Feet stand on the ground beneath the snow, so at 0% every step cuts to the bottom and anything low - a long skirt, a hand, a blade - cuts as deep as it reaches. At 50% one pass carves half of that: legs sink into the snow and the trench behind stays shallow. Every new pass over the same snow carves the same share of what is left, so busy paths sink deeper the more they are walked. Dropped items, spells and melt keep their own depths. Affects new trenches only.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_screen_spa: Community Shaders' Screen-Space Shadows on the ground snow and object snow: the small, sharp shadows where grass, feet and objects meet the snow (needs Screen-Space Shadows). Off, the snow is shaded by the sun's shadows and its own self-shadowing only. The Medium and Low presets turn it off.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_slumping_t: Snow dug away on BOTH sides loses its support and settles about halfway into a low uneven bump, so heavy traffic reads as one churned channel instead of a comb of full-height fins. Trench walls and open snow never move. 0 = off; higher = faster settling.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_texture_pa: DDS path (relative to Data) for the shell's snow diffuse. Point it at the modlist's snow texture, then press Reload.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_textured_r: Some meshes wear snow as a plain texture rather than the game's projected paint: dirt cliffs with a snow01 top, rock piles and their skirts, a season mod's winter variants, the vanilla drifts. The projected-snow recolor never sees those, so they keep their own snow texture and mismatch the shell. This gives them the shell's snow in the object's own shader, on the texels that read as snow; a plain ground snow texture (snow01, snowrocks01) takes it on every texel where it lies flat, so the stones in a rock pile's ground turn to snow too. Solid shapes also take the drape's coat over that snow; blended overlays such as rock skirts keep their own soft edge and take no coat. Needs Recolor Projected Snow.
feature.snow_deformation.snow_trenches_t: Everything about the ground being walked through: how long a trench is remembered, how wide and how sharply it cuts, and the look of the disturbed snow around it. Untouched snow is never affected.
feature.snow_deformation.speed_spoil_siz: How far the thrown snow reaches, length and width together. At 1 a sprint throws it about a metre back from each print; 0.5 is half that. Applies to new wedges.
feature.snow_deformation.speed_spoil_too: A foot leaving its print faster than a run throws snow back from it in a wedge - the faster, and the heavier the creature, the longer and stronger - and the impact detail shows that thrown snow, past the trench too, until snowfall buries it. It carves nothing; it shows which way someone was running. On the ground and on roads.
feature.snow_deformation.spell_cat_fire_: Fire melts snow into soft basins. Unlike a footprint, a melt keeps deepening for as long as the heat stands over it.
feature.snow_deformation.spell_cat_force: Force is the one school that moves snow without changing it. Everything else removes it, burns it or freezes it; a shove throws it forward and aside, deepest at the mouth and breaking up into streaks that thin out with distance, and piles what it moved along the rim. That is what makes Unrelenting Force read as pushed rather than deleted.
feature.snow_deformation.spell_cat_frost: Frost neither removes snow nor throws it aside - it refreezes what is there. Crusted snow bears weight, so tracks across it barely print; something heavy enough still breaks through. What frost looks like is the game's own frost mark, on every snow surface.
feature.snow_deformation.spell_cat_light: Lightning does not melt snow, it throws it aside and burns what is left. A discharge pocks a small core with arc legs forking off it, and unlike a melt the displaced snow still piles into a rim.
feature.snow_deformation.spell_enable_to: Lets cast magic mark the snow. Off, the melt machinery still serves campfire clearings.
feature.snow_deformation.spell_integrati: How magic marks the snow. Each school marks it differently: fire melts basins, and the others arrive with their own steps.
feature.snow_deformation.spell_melt_rate: How fast a fire stream melts down to its basin, for a spell of Flames' strength; stronger spells scale up from here. This changes how quickly the basin appears, never how deep it ends up - depth is the bowl shape below.
feature.snow_deformation.stamp_hash_ring: Writes the last 300 frames' stamp checksums to the log. Record one with a lever off and one with it on, in the same scene with the same motion; matching sequences mean the change did not touch what reaches the deformation map.
feature.snow_deformation.statics_debug_m: Object snow renders its decision data as colors with dithering disabled; missing pixels mean the geometry itself is absent. The trench patch always reads red = trample, green = skin depth (dim) plus the road bit (bright green, above half, means the road owns this column). The skins follow the selected mode. Edge taper: red = the height the taper allows, green = up-facing, blue = the raster returned no data. Coverage alpha: red = the opacity the dither sees, green = the facing gates, blue = the seam blends. Normals: red = smoothed normal z (0.5 = horizontal, 1 = straight up), green = the flat/rounded class. Self-shadow march (patch and skins alike): red = how much the march darkens the pixel, green = taps that rebuilt the road's carved surface, blue = taps that used the flat dusting, dim magenta = the march never ran here (already shadowed, or the sun too low). Projected mask (skins only, patch renders dim gray): red = the skin's own reconstruction of the game's projected-snow blend (hold it against Recolor Weight Tint with object snow off), green = how much snow the mesh's authored data wants - GRADED, so dim green means a dusting and bright green means full snow (zeroed when the draw has no projected-UV data). Yellow = agree, red-only = we place snow where the data says bare, blue = no projection data, magenta = no data but our mask fires.
feature.snow_deformation.statics_debug_v:
Paints the object snow with the decision data behind it instead of its material.

EVERY mode shows the whole snow shell, including the parts normally hidden - an object reading as one solid colour is the view working, not a problem with the snow.

Skin identity: every snow skin in its own colour, striped where the skin is drawn in the game's decal depth mode (the overlay meshes on rocks and trims). The object's own material showing through where snow should be means NO skin won that pixel's depth test - the skin is either drawn and losing, or not drawn at all (see the culling census).

Depth fight: the same test, scored. Green = a skin won the pixel, red = this skin lost it; brightness = by how many depth ULPs (dim = a hair, bright = a lot), striped as above. Green here must coincide with colour in Skin identity; a pixel coloured there but bare here means the view's bias formula is off - report it.

Volume seed (needs Volume Snow on): why the volume does or does not grow on this surface, judged the way the seed pass judges it at the nearest level. GREEN = the volume holds snow here. RED = something captured sits within the headroom above it (a beam, an eave, the member's own inside). BLUE = the surface faces too steeply for Volume Max Slope. YELLOW = seeded but weak - a door, a sheltering roof, or a closed sky; brightness is the weight. MAGENTA = seeded fine, yet no field here - the sweep, rounding or coverage threshold removed it, or a coarser ring owns this spot. Light GREY = this surface is not in the volume's occupancy at all (never captured, or thinner than a voxel). Dark grey = outside the volume's window.
feature.snow_deformation.steep_face_thin: How much less the accumulating snow spreads onto steep faces. Snow does not settle on a vertical post or wall the way it does on a roof: at 1 a vertical face takes none of the spread that Edge Lump Reach (or snowfall) adds, at 0 it takes all of it, and slopes gentler than about 60 degrees always take all of it. The game's own painted snow is never touched - with Edge Lump Reach at 0 this setting does nothing. Needs Recolor Projected Snow.
feature.snow_deformation.stored_trench_f: How long a remembered trench lasts with no snowfall at all. Snowfall does the real erasing, at the same rate it erases the ground in front of you, so a trench behaves the same whether or not you are looking at it - this is the slow floor underneath that, so a world where it never snows still forgets eventually instead of remembering for ever. 0 turns the floor off and leaves snowfall as the only thing that clears stored trenches.
feature.snow_deformation.tessellation_to: Adds vertex density to the ground snow and the road trench patch near the camera, keyed off the deformation map, so carves resolve as smooth walls instead of following the ground's own triangles. This is what trench smoothness actually depends on. Off leaves every trench as angular as the triangles beneath it.
feature.snow_deformation.texture_depths_: Every landscape texture the game has loaded this session, each with its own shell height. A texture starts at its family's default above; moving it here pins it to its own value, saved by texture path so load order cannot rebind it. Use this to give snow to textures the families lump in with bare ground (snowy stone, frozen marsh), or to hold one texture back.
feature.snow_deformation.texture_pinned: Pinned to its own value; Reset hands it back.
feature.snow_deformation.texture_shipped: Ships with its own default, so the family slider does not reach it.
feature.snow_deformation.track_ageing_to: How fast tracks age. An old track's walls round off, shallower and wider, its rim loses its teeth and lip, its berm settles, and new snow covers the broken snow and the dark wet print. Snowfall ages tracks fastest: at 1.00 an hour of it does what a day of calm cold does. Walking an old track again makes it fresh where your feet reach the floor. Ages are kept in saves. 0 = tracks never age.
feature.snow_deformation.trampled_flatte: Snow walked over again and again is packed down, and the broken snow on the trench floor is walked flatter: this multiplies Detail Relief on floors deeper than one pass leaves them, easing in the deeper the traffic has packed them. At 0.50x a Detail Relief of 1 becomes 0.5. The berms and a trail walked once are never touched. 1.00x = off.
feature.snow_deformation.trench_detail_c: How far across a trench the detail reaches. 0 = the trench floor only, 1 = the floor and walls to just past the rim, 2 = out over the berm, 2.5 = the berm's whole apron. The edge fades softly at every setting and every snow depth, and the detail fades out where a trench meets an object.
feature.snow_deformation.trench_detail_g: The shape and surface of disturbed snow: the raised berm along trench edges, the broken snow in and around trenches and the broken rim. Road trenches wear all of it; snow on objects takes the berm.
feature.snow_deformation.trench_detail_m: Trench detail textures not found: Shaders\SnowDeformation\TrenchDetailN.dds and TrenchDetailH.dds.
feature.snow_deformation.trench_detail_r: Height of the broken snow in and around trenches, on the ground and on roads. It is drawn with parallax occlusion: each pixel follows its view ray into the clods, crumbs and slabs, so nearer ones hide what lies behind them and shade it from the sun, while the snow keeps your snow texture's colour, sparkle and lighting. It eases off on thin snow and on trampled floors (Flattening). Disturbed snow wears the powder detail in every weather; where something hits it hard - a sprint, a dodge, a landing, a body knocked down, lightning, a Force shout - it turns to the impact detail, the harder the more, and rises up to 1.5x. Snow fire has melted wears the impact detail too. 1 = as authored, 0 = off.
Snow roughness where the detail applies, as a multiplier. Lower is glossier, for wet snow; 1 leaves the snow set's own roughness.
feature.snow_deformation.trench_detail_v: Paints the snow orange where the trench detail applies, over grey shading, on the ground and on roads, to judge Coverage at a glance.
feature.snow_deformation.trench_memory_t: How much the world is allowed to remember, measured as the space it will take up in your save. Past it, the ground you visited longest ago is forgotten first. 1 MB is around three thousand patches of trodden ground - far more than snowfall usually leaves standing, so weather normally clears old trenches long before this limit matters and it sits here as a backstop for weather that never comes. Note this is the SAVE cost: trench data packs down more than forty times over, so it takes far more RAM than this while you play, and every save file carries its own copy.
feature.snow_deformation.undulation_spac: Stretches the wave pattern: larger = broader, calmer dunes instead of a spike carpet.
feature.snow_deformation.undulation_stre: Wave height. 0 flattens deep snow into a smooth sheet.
feature.snow_deformation.undulation_tool: Wind-worked waves in deep snow. They fade out automatically over thin cover, class borders and carved trench floors.
feature.snow_deformation.unprojected_sha: A building whose snow is painted on by the game is drawn as several shapes, and some of them carry no snow at all. Those plain shapes are drawn over the snowy ones, and they wipe out the note the game leaves for the drape saying whether a spot was painted. With no note, the drape assumes nothing was ever decided and lays snow anyway - which is how door frames and posts under a roof end up sleeved in snow. On, a plain shape leaves the note "considered, no snow here" and the drape stays off it. Only objects with a real snow material are affected; snow-textured mesh replacements and drifts are not.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_detail_d: Inside this distance the volume snow shades with the object snow's full material. Over the next half of it the parts you cannot see at range fade out: the parallax relief marches, the berm ridges, and the five-tap horizon shadow march. Object snow itself is not affected. Raise it if far volume snow looks flatter than the object snow beside it; lower it for a cheaper draw.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_dirty_br: A rebuild recomputes the snow only in the columns of bricks whose captured shape changed since the last one - something newly seen, faded, or scrolled in - plus the blur's reach around them; everywhere else keeps last time's snow, which is world-anchored and does not move. Standing still, almost nothing is rebuilt. Every 120th rebuild is whole. Off rebuilds everything every time, for comparing.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_fine_lev: How many levels, counting out from the camera, keep the Ring Shape's full grid. The rest use half as many voxels a side at twice the voxel: the same reach for an eighth of the voxels and a fraction of the memory, and one step less detail out where it is too far to see. Changing this rebuilds those levels.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_forward_: How far ahead of you each ring's window sits, as a fraction of its width. 0 centres it on you; higher puts more of it in front, where you look, and less behind. At 0.35 each ring reaches about 85% of its width ahead of you and 15% behind. Turning around refreshes the near ring the same frame; the far rings take a few.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_levels_t: Nested grids around the camera - the clipmap. Each level is a Ring Shape window at twice the voxel of the one inside it, and draws only the ring the finer level does not reach, so the reach doubles per level while the near detail stays the base voxel. A full level takes about 226 MB at the default Wide shape (56 MB Cubic, 129 MB Wide, flat), and each level runs its own capture and field passes.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_march_st: How far apart the draw samples the snow field along each pixel's ray, in voxels. The hit is refined afterwards, so this only has to find the crossing - but a lip thinner than a step can be stepped over. Halving it doubles the draw's cost.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_max_dist: Past this the volume snow dithers out and the object snow carries the object alone. The outermost rings sample objects at their coarsest voxel, and there is a range at which the object snow's own smooth cover simply looks better than that. 8000 = never.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_max_slop: Surfaces steeper than this grow no volume snow. Read from the object's own surface normal, captured into the volume with it, so a wall is a wall whatever its stones do, and an underside never grows snow at any setting.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_ring_sha: The window every ring is cut from. Wide doubles the reach sideways and ahead for four times the memory; wide and flat halves the height for about half of Wide's memory, so eaves above you go to the next ring out. Every ring shares the shape, each still twice the one inside it in every axis.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_skip_emp: The ray jumps over the eighths of a brick that hold no snow surface instead of sampling through them. No visible change; off for comparing cost.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_sky_expo: How much the sky matters. At 100%% a spot that can see little sky grows little snow, so open ground piles deep and sheltered corners stay thin; at 0%% every surface grows the same depth.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_snow_cov: How much thinning a lip survives before it ends. Lower = longer overhangs and thin things (rails, posts) keep their caps; higher = the snow ends sooner past an edge. It does not change the depth.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_snow_dep: How high the snow surface sits over an object's top - the same on every ring, near or far, whatever that ring's voxel size. Toward an edge it rounds down over Edge Rounding.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_snow_ove: How far past an edge the snow may jut sideways, in units, whatever its depth - past this it only grows up. Also how readily the snow of two nearby surfaces melds into one. Solid always stops it - snow never spreads through a wall or up a step riser - so this is the reach across open air only. Lower keeps steps and rails distinct; higher bridges gaps and caps posts wider.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_snow_rou: How the snow rounds toward an edge: where half the neighbourhood is air the snow is this much lower, and it keeps falling smoothly past the edge into the lip. Separate from Overhang, which is where the lip is cut. On a ring whose voxels are larger than this the rounding cannot show, and there the far snow keeps its full slab instead.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_snow_too: Rasterises the captured objects into nested windows of voxels around the camera (Ring Shape, Levels), grows a snow field on every surface that faces up, and draws that field as snow - marched per pixel and shaded with the object snow's own material, so it matches the snow on the objects beneath it, which keeps drawing under it. Snow whose shape is not inherited from the object's mesh: it can overhang an edge, bridge two rocks, cap a post. Remembered between frames and fading where nothing redraws. Cost is the Volume - Bake and Volume - Draw rows.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_staggere: An object already in a ring's volume is re-drawn into it only every 8th rebuild on the nearest ring (4th and 2nd on the next two); its memory keeps it there between. Everything you have not seen yet still draws within that many rebuilds - a few frames near you. Off draws every object into every ring every rebuild, for comparing the Volume - Bake row.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_vertical: How far below the eye each ring's window sits, as a fraction of its height. The third-person camera climbs when you look down, and a window centred on it then loses the ground beside you to the next ring out - the ring colours changing with pitch. Positive puts more of the nearest ring below you, where the fences and steps are, and less above, where the eaves are.
feature.snow_deformation.volume_voxel_si: How fine the snow field is nearest the camera. Each further level doubles the voxel and doubles the reach, so detail near you and reach far from you are set separately: this slider for detail, Volume Levels for reach. Changing this restarts the volume.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_force_reb: Rebuilds every ring on its cadence even when nothing it reads has changed. Off, a ring whose window, captured objects, exclusions and settings have all held still for a memory's worth of rebuilds skips the rebuild entirely - the A/B for that gate. On while judging flicker with Dirty Bricks off, or the gate freezes the picture you are judging.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_memory_to: How long a voxel stays after its object last drew, at 60 fps. Objects behind the camera are not in the capture list, so the volume keeps what it has seen and lets it fade. An object you have not looked at since switching this on is not in the volume yet.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_occupancy: The sanity number. Geometry is surfaces, so a few percent is plausible even in a busy town; tens of percent means the volume holds something other than surfaces and the picture cannot be trusted.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_show_ring: Tints the volume snow by the ring that drew it: green, blue, yellow, magenta, cyan, red from the nearest out. The dithered hand-over bands show as a speckled mix. Not saved.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_show_slic: Draws a picture of what the volume holds.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_slice_hin:
The square is the chosen level's window - the Finest level line further up gives the finest one's size - and the cross is its centre, which sits ahead of you by Forward Bias. Red = an object surface: bright when drawn this frame, dim as it fades. Each red block is one voxel of that level.

Start with X-ray ON and a Side plane. A house should read as a box with a pitched roof, a rock as a blob. Uniform speckle with no shapes means the volume is wrong, and the number above will say so.

Then X-ray OFF for the real test: slide the Offset until the plane cuts through a porch or covered walkway, and look for the roof as a line with EMPTY space beneath it and the floor as a second line below. A thin plane prints a drifting surface as dots rather than a line - that is normal.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_slice_sou: Objects: what V0 captured. Snow field: the soft blob field grown from every object top (brighter = more snow). Snow surface: that field cut at Coverage - the shape the snow would take, before anything is drawn.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_status_fa: NOT RUNNING: a voxel shader failed to compile, or this GPU cannot run the volume - see CommunityShaders.log.
feature.snow_deformation.voxel_xray_tool: On: everything along the view direction is flattened into one image, so whole objects show as silhouettes - look at this first. Off: a single plane, one voxel thin, at the Offset - the only view that can show a roof with empty space beneath it.
feature.snow_deformation.vram_aware_map_: Video memory over budget this session, map running at

When the graphics card's free video memory budget gets smaller than what 4096 costs over 2048 (about 190 MB), the map runs at 2048 for the rest of the session: past the budget the driver moves textures to system memory and frames stall. The resolution above keeps its value. The map clears once; remembered trenches are re-injected from the store.
feature.snow_deformation.wet_snow_ice_to: Snow soaked by rain or a thaw turns greyer and stops sparkling, and the packed snow of prints and paths reads as slush. When the cold comes back, the water held in packed snow freezes: trampled paths and roads glaze over, smooth, glossy and faintly blue, until a thaw or fresh snow ends the ice. The rest of the snow takes a faint crust of the same glaze. Higher ground freezes first. Follows Snow Climate. Off, only the dark wet print remains.
feature.snow_deformation.workspace_clear: Snow height remaining in a workspace bowl, as a percent of the surrounding depth. 0 melts to the floor, 100 disables the clearing. Applies within a second.

feature.sss.mean_free_path_color_tooltip: Controls how far light goes into the subsurface in the red, green, and blue channel. It is scaled by the Mean Free Path Distance.
feature.sss.mean_free_path_distance_tool: Controls the distance that Mean Free Path Color goes into subsurface.
feature.sss.post_scatter_tooltip: Divide out albedo, blur the irradiance, multiply albedo back. Preserves texture detail.
feature.sss.pre_and_post_scatter_tooltip: Split albedo across the blur using sqrt(albedo) on each side. A physically motivated middle ground.
feature.sss.pre_scatter_tooltip: Blur the lit color directly. Fastest, but blurs albedo texture detail along with lighting.

Subsurface Scattering simulates light penetration through translucent materials like skin, creating more realistic character lighting.
This technique makes organic materials appear more lifelike and natural.

This technique creates more natural-looking terrain by adding variation to texture sampling.

Implies Thin Surface. Grass and trees with subsurface use it automatically. The NIF Effect Lighting flag also enables this independently of this checkbox, except on coat or hair materials.
feature.true_pbr.micro_shadow_strength_t: How strongly ambient occlusion darkens direct light.
feature.true_pbr.micro_shadows_tooltip: Occludes direct light with the material's ambient occlusion map, adding contact shadowing to surface detail such as seams, rivets and fabric weave.

feature.true_pbr.subsurface_balance_tool: For thin surfaces, including trees and grass, the share of subsurface light sent to the side facing away from the light, shining through; the lit side receives the rest. 0 keeps it on the lit side, 0.5 splits it equally and 1 sends all of it through. feature.true_pbr.thin_surface_tooltip: For thin surfaces, specular weights scale the complete surface reflection of each side, including grazing angles, for direct and indirect lighting. Roughness scale applies to back faces. Defaults: 0.5, 0.5, 1.0. Front and back follow mesh winding.

menu.advanced.active_shaders_tooltip: List of shaders that have been used in recent frames. Enable Shader Blocking above to use hotkeys to cycle through and block shaders for debugging. Shaders not used for ~1 second are removed from this list.
menu.advanced.avg_parallelism_tooltip_1: Average useful concurrency in this workload.
menu.advanced.avg_parallelism_tooltip_2: Roughly the worker count where adding more cores gives diminishing returns.
menu.advanced.avoid_flow_control_tooltip:
Adds D3DCOMPILE_AVOID_FLOW_CONTROL to the shader compiler flags.
Forces fxc to flatten branches into predicated ops rather than emitting dynamic flow control. Often a win for short branch bodies and uniformly-taken branches; usually a loss for long divergent branches that vanilla flow control would skip entirely.
Resets every launch. Toggling this clears the shader cache and triggers a full recompile.
menu.advanced.background_compiler_thread: Number of threads used to compile shaders during gameplay. Defaults to half of performance cores to avoid impacting the render thread. Higher values finish compilation faster but may cause stuttering.
menu.advanced.clear_shader_cache_tooltip: Clear all compiled shaders from memory. Forces recompilation of all shaders on next use.
menu.advanced.column_frame_pct_tooltip: Percentage of draw calls this frame
menu.advanced.compiler_threads_tooltip: Number of threads used to compile shaders at startup. Defaults to all logical cores minus one for OS headroom (E-cores included). Higher values finish compilation faster but may make the system less responsive.
menu.advanced.compute_tooltip: Replace Compute Shaders. When false, will disable the custom Compute Shaders for the types above. For developers to test whether CS shaders match vanilla behavior.
menu.advanced.content_store_clear_toolti: Deletes every stored shader. Use this if a shader looks wrong after being restored; the next compile rebuilds the store from scratch. Shaders already in the shader cache are kept.
menu.advanced.content_store_hits: Restored since the last cache clear: {count}
menu.advanced.content_store_limit_toolti: Least recently used shaders are deleted once the store exceeds this. A full build stores about 120 MB, or about 1.1 GB in Developer Mode, so keep several builds' worth if you switch branches.
menu.advanced.content_store_tooltip:
Keeps every compiled shader keyed by its preprocessed source and compiler flags. After a cache wipe, a plugin update or a feature change, shaders already compiled for the same code are restored instead of recompiled.
Costs one preprocess per shader (tens of milliseconds) and disk space in Data/ShaderCache/ContentStore, trimmed to the least recently used. Takes effect for shaders compiled from now on.
menu.advanced.copy_info_tooltip: Copy complete shader information including cache path to clipboard
menu.advanced.developer_mode_via_log_lev: Currently active because Log Level is debug/trace.
menu.advanced.dump_feature_defaults: Dump All Feature Defaults to JSON
menu.advanced.dump_feature_defaults_tool: Writes every feature's built-in default settings to FeatureDefaults.json and opens it. Defaults come from the running build; Baseline packs and your edits are not included.
menu.advanced.dump_shaders_tooltip: Dump shaders at startup. This should be used only when reversing shaders. Normal users don't need this.
menu.advanced.enable_developer_mode_tool: Unlocks developer-only options and tooling. Also enabled automatically when Log Level is debug or trace. Use at your own risk.
menu.advanced.enable_file_watcher_toolti: Automatically recompile shaders on file change. Intended for developing.
menu.advanced.enable_shader_blocking_too: Enables hotkeys to cycle through and block individual shaders for debugging purposes.
menu.advanced.frame_annotations_tooltip: Enable detailed frame annotations for debugging render passes and draw calls.
menu.advanced.half_precision_tooltip:
Adds D3DCOMPILE_PARTIAL_PRECISION to the shader compiler flags.
Lets fxc downgrade unmarked float ops to FP16 where it can prove safety, on top of the existing min16float type hints.
On FP16-capable GPUs (Pascal+ / GCN+ / Skylake+) this can halve register pressure and double ALU throughput, but it can also introduce minor visual differences in shaders that haven't been audited for precision sensitivity.
Toggling this clears the shader cache and triggers a full recompile.
menu.advanced.infinite_core_efficiency_t: How close runtime is to the infinite-core lower bound.
menu.advanced.infinite_core_gap_tooltip_: Defined as 100 * (1 - S / T_p). Lower is better.
menu.advanced.log_level_tooltip: Log level. Trace is most verbose. Default is info. Debug and Trace also enable Developer Mode.

menu.faq.a1: Community Shaders is a comprehensive graphics enhancement framework for Skyrim that provides advanced lighting, materials, and visual effects. It's designed to be modular, allowing you to enable only the features you want while maintaining good performance.
menu.faq.a2: Each feature can be found in the left sidebar menu. Click on any feature to access its settings. Most features include presets and detailed tooltips to help you understand what each setting does.
menu.faq.a3: Features may fail to load due to hardware incompatibility, missing dependencies, or conflicts with other mods. Check the 'Feature Issues' tab for detailed information about any problematic features.
menu.faq.a4: Failed shaders are usually caused by mixed file versions. Ensure all features are up to date and avoid mixing files from test builds or outdated versions. Please review the 'Feature Issues' tab and/or Wiki for more information. Update your features and remove any obsolete features.
menu.faq.a5: Start by enabling the Performance Overlay to monitor your FPS. Consider disabling expensive features like Screen Space GI or reducing quality settings. The 'Display' tab also includes upscaling options that can improve performance.
menu.faq.a6: No, Community Shaders is not compatible with ENB. Community Shaders will automatically disable itself if ENB is detected.
menu.faq.a7: By default, Community Shaders uses the END key to open this menu. If your keyboard doesn't have an END key or it's not working, you can change it in the General > Keybindings tab. You can also edit the hotkey in the JSON configuration files.
menu.faq.a8: We're always looking for talented developers to join the team! Check out our GitHub wiki for contribution guidelines and join our Discord server to connect with the development team. Whether you're interested in shader programming, C++ development, or documentation, there's always something to contribute.
menu.faq.a9: Yes! Community Shaders is completely open source and available on GitHub. You can view the source code, report issues, suggest features, and contribute to the project. The project is licensed under GPL, ensuring it remains free and open for everyone. Branding materials and assets (icons, nexus branding, typography, etc) are not covered by the GPL Licence. Any included assets may not be used without explicit permission.
